tx.t: In this lecture we will look at the diversity of languages around the world. There are about seven thousand languages spoken today.
About forty per cent of them are endangered, which means they are at risk of disappearing. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, while English is the most widely spoken language overall.
Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country, with more than eight hundred languages. Just twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population.
A language usually disappears when children stop learning it at home.

tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.
A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

tx.t: Today I will explain how the human heart works. The heart has four chambers: two at the top, called atria, and two at the bottom, called ventricles.
At rest, the adult heart beats between sixty and one hundred times every minute. Over a day, that adds up to roughly one hundred thousand beats.
The heart pumps about five litres of blood around the body every minute. The heart of an adult weighs only about three hundred grams, and it is about the size of a clenched fist.

tx.t: Today we look at how printing changed the world. Before printing, every book in Europe was copied by hand, usually by monks, which took months.
Around fourteen forty, a German goldsmith called Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press with movable metal letters. The famous Gutenberg Bible was printed around fourteen fifty-five.
William Caxton set up the first printing press in England in fourteen seventy-six. By the year fifteen hundred, historians estimate that more than twenty million books had been printed in Europe.
Cheaper books helped literacy spread and made it easier to share new scientific ideas.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Fenwick. It began in twenty thirteen with eight hundred and thirty-eight bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by sixty-two per cent, and on a busy day there were more than twenty-four thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: empty stations at rush hour. The council solved it with a mobile app that shows where bikes are available.
Today, a ride costs two pounds seventy-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: Today we are going to look at Antarctica, the coldest continent. About ninety-eight per cent of Antarctica is covered in ice.

The lowest temperature ever recorded on Earth, minus eighty-nine degrees Celsius, was measured there at Vostok Station in nineteen eighty-three. The ice contains about seventy per cent of the world's fresh water.

No people are native to Antarctica. Only scientists live there, and their numbers change with the seasons. The Antarctic Treaty of nineteen fifty-nine, signed by twelve countries, says that the continent can be used only for peaceful purposes and science.
Penguins, seals and whales live around its coasts.

The students who used the method of studying at the same time each day felt less stressed before the exam. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.
